Chapter 1
Claude Code & Figma
Your block, ~25 min. Quick intro to Claude Code and the desktop app, a five-minute run-through for anyone not set up yet, then connect Figma. Keep it calm, this is the part people arrive nervous about.

What is Claude Code?

Claude chat (claude.ai)
✓Great for talking things through and quick answers
✕Can't open your project or touch your files
✕You copy code out by hand and paste it back
Claude Code (desktop app)
✓Reads your Figma file and your project directly
✓Writes and edits real files, builds a running interface
✓Runs in a normal window, no terminal needed
Same Claude underneath. The difference is that Claude Code can actually do the thing, not just describe it.
Two minutes, plain language. Open the desktop app live and show a new chat. If anyone still hasn't installed it, this is the five-minute run-through: download from claude.com/download, sign in with the paid plan, say hello. Mention where Claude Code shines: design-to-code, real projects, repeatable edits, not one-off answers.

VS Code

A free code editor from Microsoft. It's where you open your project and see the real files Claude Code builds.

1Go to code.visualstudio.com and download the build for your computer.
2Install it like any app, then open it once to check it launches.
Quick, everyone follows along. Show the download page live, pick the right build, install, open. This is the last install before we start building. On a Mac, drag it into Applications after unzipping.

Connect Figma to Claude Code

1In the desktop app, find the Figma connector.

Chapter 2
The Handoff
Fifteen minutes, no build. The whole chapter argues one point: the model is not the variable, your file is. Keep energy up, they have just been installing things.

Paste a design in, get a working product out.

The promise
Say it as though you believe it. Ask for hands: "Who has tried this and got something you would actually ship?" Usually two or three hands, then qualified. Let the silence do the work before you turn the slide.

What Actually Happens

The model reproduces the structure you give it. Whatever that structure is.

A screenshot goes in
✕Unnamed layers become guessed structure
✕Sampled colors become hardcoded hex
✕No states means one static view
✕A change request becomes a rewrite
A system goes in
✓Named components become named code
✓Tokens become variables
✓Defined states become states in the build
✓A change request becomes one value
The spine of the whole workshop. Both columns used the same model and the same prompt. The only variable that moved is the file. Land it: "Nobody in this room is getting worse output because they have a worse model."

Your design system is the prompt.

The reframe
The one sentence they should repeat to a colleague tomorrow. Say it, pause, say it again. Then the consequence: every hour spent on naming and tokens is now prompt engineering, whether you call it that or not.

What The Model Reads

Five inputs. You control all five, and four of them live in Figma.

Layer and component names
Nesting and structure
Token values and their names
The states you drew
The rules file you wrote
→
Model
→
A working interface

Everything it gets right, you gave it. Everything it invents, you left blank.

Colour code is consistent all night: purple is input, yellow is the model, green is output. Point out that the middle box is the only one they cannot edit. No yellow tab on this slide, the model node is already the yellow.

Naming Is Functional

What you shipped
✕Frame 427
✕Rectangle 12 copy
✕Result: a component no one can name, referenced nowhere, rebuilt every time it appears.
What it needed
✓Badge/Status/Open
✓Card/Metric/Positive
✓Result: one component, four variants, referenced by name everywhere it appears.
Rename before you prompt. It is the cheapest thing you will do tonight.
Concrete, and slightly embarrassing. Ask them to open any recent client file and read three layer names aloud in their head. Nobody volunteers. That is the point. This is the moment to say renaming is not admin, it is the spec.

The Rules File

One file the model reads on every single run, so you stop repeating yourself in chat.

Layer 01
Sources of truth
Where the tokens live. Which components are canonical. Which frame is the reference for this screen.
Layer 02
Constraints
Spacing comes from the scale. Type comes from the five steps. Every interactive element ships with its states.
Layer 03
Never
No new colors. No hardcoded values. No one-off overrides to make a single screen look right.
Show the actual file for ten seconds if the room is technical enough, otherwise stay on the slide. The third card is the one they underestimate: without a "never" list the model is helpful in exactly the wrong way. Tell them the template is in the take-home pack.

Why Systems Pay

671%
Return on investment measured for design system implementation in studied organisations.
Forrester TEI, design systems
98 min
Saved per developer, per week, after design system adoption in a studied organisation.
Forrester TEI
The system was never overhead. It is the thing that compounds.
Two numbers, no more. These are for the designer who has to justify system work to a founder or a PM on Monday. Say the second payout plainly: the same file that saved a developer's week now steers the model. Do not add numbers that are not on this slide.
Chapter 3
The Build
35 minutes, hands on keyboards. Vidushi takes tooling failures, I take design decisions. Announce the split out loud so people know who to flag. Target: everyone clears build 3 by 18:50, build 4 is the last ten minutes.

The Four Builds

  1. 01One componentBuild Button/Primary with its variants. Proves the token path is real and not a coincidence.
  2. 02One blockBuild the metric row from the component you just made. Proves reuse, and catches the model quietly cloning instead of referencing.
  3. 03The screen, with statesEmpty, loading, error. Proves the part nobody gets for free, because nobody asks for it.
  4. 04The change requestOne token moves. Proves whether you built a system or a very tidy screenshot.
Read build 4 last and slowly. That is the build the evening is built around. Everything before it is setup for that moment. If the room is running late, cut build 2, never build 4.
Hands onChapter 3 · The Build

Build It, Then Change It

1Open the starter file and read the component names before you prompt. Build Button/Primary and check: did the colour arrive as a token or a hex?
2Build the metric row, then the full screen with its empty, loading and error states.
3Open the Change Request frame. Change one token, change nothing else. Watch whether the whole screen follows.
4If you had to touch a component to get there, your system leaked. Find exactly where.
50 minutes, two moves in one block. First they build (component → block → full screen with states); then the change request is the payoff, do it live on the projector first in one edit. If the screen follows, the system held; if they touch five files, it leaked, and that is the real lesson. Step 4 is the teaching: collect two or three leak locations to reuse in the critique chapter. Hard stop at 19:00 whatever state they are in.
Chapter 4
The Critique
My hour. Twenty minutes teaching the method, thirty minutes of them running it on their own build, ten minutes of showing two or three on the projector. This is the part that makes the evening a design workshop rather than a tools class.

Plausible, Not Correct

What you get for free
✓A layout that reads at a glance
✓Colors that are roughly the right colors
✓Copy sitting in the right places
✓Something you could screenshot and post
What you never get unless you ask
✕Spacing that holds the scale instead of drifting
✕Hierarchy that survives real content lengths
✕The states nobody drew
✕A visible focus ring and a usable target size
The right column is your job. It is also the part that is not automated.
Do not let this sound anti-AI. The left column is genuinely valuable and took a week five years ago. The argument is about where the designer's scarcity moved, not about whether the tool is good. Watch the tone here, the room contains both evangelists and sceptics.

Six Passes

  1. 01TokensIs every value coming from the system, or has something been hardcoded?
  2. 02StructureAre these your named components, or lookalikes rebuilt from scratch?
  3. 03HierarchyDoes the eye land where the design sent it, with real content in place?
  4. 04StatesHover, focus, disabled, empty, loading, error. All six, every time.
  5. 05ResponsiveWhat breaks at 390 pixels wide, and what silently overflows?
  6. 06Accessibility floorContrast, visible focus, target size, and semantics that match the meaning.
The reference slide of the evening. Leave it up during their critique block. Justify the order with one example: fixing spacing on a component that should not exist wastes the fix twice. Tell them this checklist is in the take-home pack, so nobody photographs it.

The Critique Prompt

Hand the model your checklist and make it audit its own work against the frame.

Compare the current build against the frame Inbox/Desktop. Run these six passes, in order: tokens · structure · hierarchy · states · responsive · accessibility For each pass, list what fails and the exact file and line. Do not fix anything yet. I will decide what gets fixed.
Separate finding from fixing. The finding can be delegated. The decision cannot.
The last line is the whole slide. If you let it fix while it finds, you lose the review and inherit changes you never read. Demo the difference live if there is time: same build, with and without the final line. This prompt ships in the take-home pack.

The Two Traps

Trap one
✕A component named Group 12
✕It compiled. It rendered. It looks correct on screen, and nobody on your team can reference it, extend it or find it again.
Trap two
✕One card using #2E7D32 instead of a token
✕It survived build four untouched. Every other card followed the change. That one card is now permanently wrong.

Neither of these is a model failure. Both are handoff failures, and both were yours to catch.

The best five minutes of the night if you time it right. Do not reveal the traps until at least one person has found one on their own, then credit them by name. If nobody found them, that is a stronger point, not a weaker one.
Hands onChapter 4 · The Critique

Run The Six Passes

1Run the critique prompt against your own build. Read the whole list before you touch anything.
2Fix passes one and two only. Tokens and structure. Leave the surface alone.
3Re-run the pass. Notice how many surface problems fixed themselves.
Thirty minutes. Walk the room the whole time. Step 3 is the lesson: most hierarchy and spacing complaints disappear once structure is right. Pick two builds to show at 19:50, ask permission first. Warn the room at 19:45 that we are wrapping.

What's Next
Ten minutes, high energy, then questions. The job of this chapter is to stop the evening being a fun night that changes nothing in your real work.

What You Take Home

Sent within 48 hours. Keep the files and reuse them after tonight.

The starter Figma file · design system, components, all states
The rules file template · sources of truth, constraints, never
The four build prompts · one for each build
The six-pass critique checklist · plus the critique prompt
The troubleshooting guide · the eight failures we saw tonight
Say "within 48 hours" and then actually do it. This is the credibility promise from the Luma page. Mention that the troubleshooting guide is written after tonight, from tonight's actual failures, not a generic list.

After Tonight

  1. 01Pick a screen you already designedNot a new idea. Something shipped, something real, something you already know is right.
  2. 02Rename it properly and write the rules fileOne hour, no code. This is the part everyone skips and the part that decides the result.
  3. 03Build one component, then ask for the change requestIf the change propagates, your system is real. If it does not, you found the leak in an hour instead of a quarter.
If step two feels slow, that is the work. It is also the return.
Be specific about the hour. Designers will not start a system rewrite, but they will spend one hour renaming one screen. That is the wedge. Offer the room a follow-up: send me what you built in a week.

Questions.

Thirty minutes, both hosts. Prepared answers ready for: "does this replace developers", "what about a codebase that already exists", "which models", "what if we have no design system at all". Close by naming where the files will arrive and from which address.
